cues.text: A Council Calls for a New Catechism
The idea of a new, universal catechism for the whole Catholic Church emerged from the Extraordinary Synod of Bishops convened by Pope John Paul II in 1985.
The synod marked the twentieth anniversary of the close of the Second Vatican Council.
Reflecting on two decades of the Council's implementation, the assembled bishops called for a single authoritative compendium of Catholic doctrine.
It could serve as a reliable reference point for the many national and diocesan catechisms then in use across the world.
Six Years of Drafting
John Paul II entrusted the project to a commission of twelve cardinals and bishops chaired by Cardinal Joseph Ratzinger , Prefect of the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith.
Ratzinger oversaw an extensive drafting and consultation process incorporating feedback from bishops' conferences around the world across multiple successive drafts.
This genuinely global undertaking intended to produce a text reflecting the Church's teaching with both doctrinal precision and pastoral clarity.
The First Universal Catechism Since Trent
John Paul II promulgated the Catechism of the Catholic Church on October 11, 1992, the thirtieth anniversary of the opening of the Second Vatican Council.
He described it as a compendium intended to serve bishops and all the Christian faithful as a sure and authentic reference text for teaching Catholic doctrine.
It was the first new universal catechism the Church had produced since the Roman Catechism commissioned by the Council of Trent over four centuries earlier.
Structured Around Four Pillars

The new Catechism organized the whole of Catholic teaching around four traditional pillars: the Creed (what the Church believes) and the sacraments (how the Church worships and celebrates the mysteries of faith).
The pillars also include the moral life (how the Church calls believers to live, organized around the Ten Commandments) and prayer (how the Church prays, organized around the Lord's Prayer).
This structure was drawn directly from the pattern of the earlier Roman Catechism, adapted to address the doctrinal and pastoral questions of the contemporary Church.
Legacy
A definitive Latin typical edition followed in 1997, correcting and refining the text of the original vernacular editions.

Since then, the Catechism has been translated into dozens of languages, becoming a standard reference for bishops, catechists, and ordinary believers seeking an authoritative and accessible account of Catholic teaching.
Pope John Paul II himself described the work as a genuine gift to the whole Church.
Three decades after Vatican II, it offered a single reliable compendium capable of guiding the Council's continued reception into ordinary Catholic belief and practice.
